asset-finance|manufacturing.title: Asset Finance for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
asset-finance|manufacturing.desc: How hire purchase and leasing work for UK manufacturers buying CNC machines, presses and production lines. One short form matches you with a specialist broker.
asset-finance|manufacturing.lead: Spread the cost of a machine tool or production line over its working life, with the equipment itself acting as the security.
intro: A machine tool earns its keep over ten or fifteen years, but the invoice arrives on day one. Asset finance lets a manufacturer pay for a CNC machine, press brake, injection moulder or packing line in instalments while it starts producing. The machine is usually the security, so lenders look hard at what it is, who built it and what it would fetch if sold second-hand. Lenders also want to see that the machine will be busy, so a signed order or a clear pipeline for the work it will do carries weight.

For example, a precision engineering firm adding a £180,000 five-axis machining centre might use hire purchase to own it at the end, or a lease if it expects to upgrade sooner. Deposits, terms and structures vary by lender and by equipment, and a broker who knows industrial kit can explain which structures suit the machine and your order book. Whichever route you choose, it is worth asking early about deposits, delivery timing and what happens at the end of the agreement. The broker will explain how deposits, residual payments and the end-of-term options differ between lenders.
uses: Replacing an ageing machine
Swap a worn lathe or press for one that holds tighter tolerances and breaks down less, without a large one-off payment.
Adding capacity for a new contract
Buy a second line or an extra machine when a customer commits to volumes your current kit cannot reach.
Automation and robotics
Finance a robot cell, a bar feeder or a vision inspection system that cuts labour per part and improves consistency.
Raising cash from machines you own
Borrow against equipment that is already paid for and use the money for materials, staff or a new line elsewhere.
fit: Standard kit versus specialist machinery

Widely used machines from established makers are easier to value, so lenders may offer longer terms and smaller deposits. One-off or heavily customised equipment has a narrow resale market, which can mean a larger deposit or a shorter term.
Matching the term to the machine’s life

Terms commonly run from two to seven years, and lenders usually keep the term inside the machine’s useful life. A broker can compare hire purchase, where you own the machine at the end, with leasing, where you may hand it back or keep paying to extend.
Delivery, installation and staged payments

Big machines often arrive months after ordering and need foundations, power and commissioning. Some lenders will pay the supplier in stages and some will include installation, so it is worth raising early rather than after the order is placed.
considerations: Total cost over the term
Spreading the price adds interest and sometimes fees, so the total paid is higher than the cash price. Ask for the full repayment figure and compare it with what the machine will earn.
You may not own the machine
With leasing, ownership usually stays with the lender, and there may be conditions on use, servicing and condition at the end. Check what happens if you want to sell the machine or move site.
Not ideal for running costs
Asset finance pays for equipment, not for materials, wages or a gap in cash flow. For those, a broker might suggest invoice finance or a revolving facility instead.
faqs: Can I finance a used or reconditioned machine?

Yes, many lenders will consider used and reconditioned machinery, particularly from known makers. They tend to look at the age, condition and whether it can be independently valued. Older equipment may be financed over a shorter term or with a larger deposit than a new machine.
Will the lender pay for installation and training?

Some will include delivery, installation and commissioning in the amount financed, others will only fund the machine itself. It depends on the lender and the supplier’s quote. Ask your broker early, because the answer can change how much deposit you need to put in.
What is the difference between hire purchase and a lease?

With hire purchase you make regular payments and become the owner at the end. With a lease the lender keeps ownership, and you may return the machine, extend the lease or sometimes buy it. Accounting and tax treatment can differ, so check with your accountant.
Can I use machines I already own as security?

Often yes. Lenders can advance money against equipment that is owned outright, sometimes through a sale and leaseback, where you sell the machine and lease it back. The amount depends on its valuation and condition. It releases cash but adds a repayment commitment.
How do lenders judge a manufacturer’s application?

They look at your trading history, accounts and the equipment itself. For larger amounts they may ask about your order book and the customers the machine will serve. Strong, steady contracts can help show that the repayments are affordable. A clear explanation of the machine’s purpose helps.

invoice-finance|manufacturing.title: Invoice Finance for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|manufacturing.desc: How invoice finance works for UK manufacturers waiting 60 to 90 days on large trade customers. One short form matches you with a specialist broker. Free to use.
invoice-finance|manufacturing.lead: Release cash from invoices to big trade customers so materials and wages are paid while you wait for them to settle.
intro: A manufacturer pays for steel, resin or components and wages up front, then sends the finished goods to a customer that pays in 60 or 90 days. Invoice finance closes that gap. Once you have invoiced, a lender advances a large share of the invoice value straight away and pays the balance, less its charges, when your customer settles. The lender’s main question is how reliably your customers pay, so the quality of your buyers matters more than the size of your own balance sheet, and long terms are the very thing it is designed to ease.

This tends to suit businesses selling to a handful of larger buyers, such as retailers, contractors or other manufacturers, where the invoices are sizeable and the customers are creditworthy. For example, a furniture maker invoicing £90,000 to a national retailer on 90-day terms could draw cash on that invoice rather than waiting. It only covers goods already delivered and invoiced, so it is a different tool from finance for machinery.
uses: Buying materials for the next order
Use cash from last month’s invoices to pay suppliers who want payment in 30 days or on order.
Bridging long retailer terms
Smooth out cash flow when a major customer pays on 90 days but your own suppliers and staff do not wait that long.
Taking on a bigger contract
Release cash as you invoice so a large order does not stall because earlier invoices are still unpaid.
Export orders
Finance invoices to overseas customers where longer payment terms are normal, if the lender is willing to cover the country concerned.
fit: Whole ledger or selected invoices

Whole-ledger facilities cover all your trade invoices and suit steady, regular billing. Selective facilities let you choose which invoices to finance, which can suit a manufacturer with one or two big customers and otherwise comfortable cash flow.
Concentration and customer quality

If one customer makes up most of your sales, lenders look closely at that customer’s payment record and may cap how much they will advance against it. Spreading sales across several buyers usually makes the facility easier to set up.
Stage payments and work in progress

Invoice finance only works once an invoice exists. If your contracts bill on milestones, the lender can finance each milestone invoice, but not the materials and labour that go in before it is raised.
considerations: Disputes and returns
If a customer disputes quality or sends goods back, the related invoice may be pulled from the facility and the cash repaid. Clear specifications and signed delivery notes reduce the chance of this.
Cost and visibility
You pay a service fee and a charge on the cash advanced, and some arrangements tell customers that a lender is involved. Confidential facilities exist, so ask which type the broker is describing.
Not for long-term investment
Invoice finance releases working capital, not capital for machinery or premises. Use it to ease cash flow, and ask a broker about asset finance for equipment.
faqs: Which manufacturers suit invoice finance?

It usually suits manufacturers invoicing other businesses on credit terms of 30 days or more, with invoices of meaningful size. Businesses selling mainly to consumers, or taking payment on order, have little to finance. Customer quality matters more than your own balance sheet. A broker can say which lenders are happy with single-customer exposure and what they would cap.
Can I finance only one big customer’s invoices?

Often yes, through a selective or single-debtor facility. The lender will focus on that customer’s credit standing and payment record. You get cash against those invoices while leaving the rest of your sales outside the arrangement. It is worth asking what share they would advance.
Will my customers know?

In some arrangements the lender collects payment and customers are told. In confidential facilities you keep collecting and the customer sees nothing different. Confidential options may need a stronger trading record, and the charges can differ. Ask the broker which type is being offered and how any customer contact would be handled.
What if a customer pays late or not at all?

With recourse facilities, you may have to repay the advance if the customer does not pay. Non-recourse protection, often through credit insurance, can cover some customer failure but costs extra and has conditions. Ask exactly what is covered. The cost and terms of that cover vary, so ask what is included.
Does invoice finance work with other borrowing?

It can, but lenders will want to know about existing security. If a bank already holds a charge over your debtors, they may need to agree or be repaid first. A broker can explain how a new facility would sit alongside your other finance.

revolving-credit-facility|manufacturing.title: Revolving Credit Facilities for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|manufacturing.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps UK manufacturers manage raw material costs and uneven order cycles. One short form matches you with a specialist broker.
revolving-credit-facility|manufacturing.lead: A credit limit you draw on to buy materials when you need them and repay as customers pay, paying charges on what you use.
intro: Raw material prices move, suppliers offer better prices for bulk, and orders rarely arrive evenly. A revolving credit facility gives a manufacturer an agreed limit to draw on when needed. You repay when cash comes in, and the available credit is restored for the next draw. Charges are based on how much you have borrowed and for how long. The limit is agreed at the start, and you only pay charges on what is drawn at any time, which keeps costs lower in quiet months than a loan for the same sum.

For example, a manufacturer of garden products might take a £150,000 facility to buy components in January for spring orders, then repay as retailers settle in May and June. Because the money is repeatedly drawn and repaid, it suits recurring swings in stock and materials. It is not designed for one-off purchases such as a machine, where a fixed-term arrangement usually fits better. and works best when you can see when each draw will be cleared. A broker can tell you which lenders tend to be comfortable with manufacturers and how they usually set a limit.
uses: Buying in bulk at a better price
Take up a supplier’s volume discount or lock in a price before an expected rise, then repay from sales.
Building stock for a seasonal peak
Pay for materials and labour in the quiet months so finished goods are ready when orders land.
Covering a long production run
Bridge the weeks between paying suppliers and shipping, particularly on made-to-order work with deposits that do not cover costs.
A buffer for late customer payments
Keep wages and supplier payments on schedule when a large customer pays later than usual.
fit: How lenders set the limit

Lenders usually base the limit on turnover, trading history and how steadily the business generates cash. Some facilities are secured against stock, debtors or other assets, which can raise the limit. Others are unsecured and typically smaller.
Matching the facility to the cycle

The benefit comes from drawing and repaying within the production cycle. If you are borrowing the full limit all year and never clearing it, it is acting like a permanent loan, and a broker may suggest a term loan for that part of the need.
Fees, reviews and covenants

Expect an arrangement fee, possibly a fee for unused credit, and an annual review of the limit. Some facilities carry conditions on your accounts, such as minimum cash or limits on other borrowing, so read these before you sign.
considerations: Limits can change
Lenders may reduce or review the limit, particularly if trading weakens or material costs push your accounts into a different position. Do not rely on a facility being at the same size indefinitely.
Repayment discipline
Because the credit comes back as you repay, it is easy to treat it as spare cash. Track what is drawn against specific orders so you know when it should be cleared.
Wrong tool for equipment
Funding a machine or a building from a revolving facility ties up the limit you need for materials. Asset finance or a secured loan is usually a better match for those costs.
faqs: How is a revolving facility different from an overdraft?

Both let you borrow up to a limit. An overdraft sits on your current account and is usually repayable on demand. A revolving credit facility is typically a separate, committed agreement with set terms and review dates. Details vary by lender, so ask which type is being offered.
Can I draw on it whenever I want?

Usually yes, within the limit and the facility’s conditions, often by request through the lender’s online system. Some lenders require notice or limit how often you can draw. Check whether drawings need to be tied to specific purchases or invoices.
Will I be charged if I don’t use it?

Some lenders charge a commitment fee on the unused part of the limit, and some only charge on what you draw. There may also be an arrangement fee and review fees. Your broker should explain which apply before you decide.
Is security needed?

Not always. Smaller facilities can be unsecured, though directors may be asked for personal guarantees. Larger facilities are often secured against debtors, stock or other business assets. The structure affects the limit and how the lender monitors it. Ask the broker which structure fits your accounts.
Can I have this alongside invoice finance?

Sometimes, but lenders will want to avoid two parties holding claims over the same assets. A broker can check how a facility and an invoice finance arrangement would fit together, or whether one of them would cover your needs on its own.

secured-business-loans|manufacturing.title: Secured Business Loans for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|manufacturing.desc: How secured business loans work for UK manufacturers, using premises or plant as security for larger sums over longer terms. Matched with a specialist broker.
secured-business-loans|manufacturing.lead: Borrow a larger sum over a longer term by offering property, plant or other business assets as security.
intro: Some manufacturing projects are too big for an unsecured loan: an extension to the factory floor, a new production hall, the purchase of a rival’s order book or a full line refit. A secured business loan offers the lender a legal charge over an asset, which can mean larger amounts and longer terms than lending without security. That charge is what lets lenders consider sums and terms that a business of your size could not usually get without it.

For manufacturers the security is often the unit or factory, machinery owned outright or a director’s property. For example, a fabricator that owns its works might borrow £600,000 against it to fund a second shift’s worth of equipment and extra stock. The lender will want a valuation, and the asset can be at risk if repayments are missed, so the loan needs to fit comfortably within the cash the business generates.
uses: Extending or fitting out the factory
Add floor space, mezzanines, extraction or three-phase power to raise output from a site you already own.
Buying out a competitor or its assets
Fund the purchase of a smaller rival, its machinery or its customer list where the price is larger than you can pay from cash.
Consolidating several borrowings
Replace a collection of smaller loans with one arrangement and a single monthly payment, if the numbers work.
Funding a long contract
Cover materials, wages and tooling for a multi-year programme where income arrives gradually.
fit: What lenders accept as security

Freehold or long leasehold property is the most widely accepted, followed by plant and machinery with a clear second-hand market. Specialist-built premises or very niche equipment can be valued more cautiously, which may reduce the amount offered.
Loan to value and the equity you hold

Lenders usually lend a percentage of the asset’s value rather than the full amount, and take any existing charges into account. If a bank already holds a charge, a second charge may be possible, but it depends on the first lender.
Terms and repayment structure

Secured loans commonly run for longer than unsecured ones, sometimes up to ten years or more for property-backed borrowing. Some include a capital repayment holiday, which can help when a project takes months to start earning.
considerations: The security is at risk
If the business cannot keep up repayments, the lender may take action against the asset. Think about how a fall in orders would affect your ability to pay before pledging the factory or the machines.
Valuation and legal costs
Expect a valuation, legal work and possibly arrangement fees, which can take time and add cost. These are usually higher than for unsecured loans, so factor them into the real cost of borrowing.
Personal guarantees and directors’ homes
Some lenders ask for a director’s personal guarantee or a charge over a personal property. Make sure you understand what that means and take independent legal advice if needed.
faqs: Can I use machinery as security for a loan?

Yes, plant and machinery can be used if it is owned outright, has a clear market value and is not already pledged to another lender. The amount depends on the independent valuation. Specialist or older machines may be valued conservatively.
What if my factory already has a mortgage?

A second charge may be possible, depending on the equity in the property and whether the first lender allows it. Lenders look at the combined borrowing against the building’s value. A broker can compare second charge options with refinancing the existing loan.
How large a loan can a manufacturer get?

It depends on the value of the security, your trading history and what the business can afford to repay. Secured loans can reach into the millions for property-backed borrowing, but there is no fixed figure. Lenders assess each case on its own facts.
How long does a valuation take?

It varies with the type of asset and the surveyor’s availability. Specialist industrial property and machinery can take longer to value than standard assets. Ask your broker what to expect, and have title documents and recent accounts ready to avoid delay.
Is a secured loan better than asset finance?

They suit different needs. Asset finance usually funds a particular machine with that machine as security. A secured loan raises a general sum against property or assets, and can be used more flexibly. A broker can explain which fits your project.

unsecured-business-loans|manufacturing.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|manufacturing.desc: How unsecured business loans work for UK manufacturers: tooling, accreditation, product development and skills, without pledging property or machinery.
unsecured-business-loans|manufacturing.lead: Fund tooling, certification and product development without putting the factory or machines up as security.
intro: Not every manufacturing cost comes with something a lender can take as security. Tooling for a new product, an ISO or aerospace accreditation, prototyping, a skilled hire or a software system for the shop floor all add capability but leave little to sell. An unsecured business loan is a fixed sum repaid in instalments, with no charge over your premises or equipment. The loan is repaid in fixed instalments, so the benefit needs to show up in orders or margins within a realistic time.

Because nothing backs the loan, lenders rely on your accounts, trading record and how comfortably the business can afford the payments. Directors are often asked for a personal guarantee. For example, a plastics moulder spending £60,000 on new tools and a trial production run might choose this route to keep its machines free for future asset finance. Lenders will still expect you to show the work or contracts the spend is meant to win.
uses: Tooling and moulds for a new product
Pay for dies, jigs or moulds that are specific to a customer’s part and have little value on resale.
Accreditation and testing
Cover audit, certification and testing costs for standards such as ISO 9001 or sector approvals that open larger customers.
Product development and prototyping
Fund design time, prototypes and trial batches before the first production order arrives.
Hiring and training skilled staff
Recruit a machinist, welder or quality engineer ahead of the extra work they will bring in.
fit: Typical amounts and terms

Unsecured loans for smaller manufacturers often fall between about £10,000 and a few hundred thousand pounds, repaid over one to five years. The amount is driven by turnover, profit and existing borrowing rather than by assets.
What lenders look at

Expect questions about filed accounts, recent bank statements, current debts and whether profits comfortably cover the repayment. A clear explanation of what the money is for, and how it will pay for itself, helps.
Keeping assets free for other finance

Borrowing without security leaves machinery and property unencumbered, so they remain available for asset finance or a secured loan later. This matters if you plan a larger purchase in the next year or two.
considerations: Personal guarantees
Lenders commonly ask directors to guarantee unsecured loans personally. That means your own assets could be at risk if the company cannot pay, so understand the terms before agreeing.
Cost compared with secured borrowing
Without security, the lender takes more risk and charges and amounts reflect it. For a purchase a machine can secure, asset finance is often more suitable.
Fixed repayments in a lumpy business
Monthly instalments continue even if orders dip. If your income is uneven, consider whether a revolving facility, which you repay as cash arrives, would be easier to manage.
faqs: Can I use an unsecured loan to buy machinery?

You can, but it is often not the best fit. A machine can usually act as its own security under asset finance, which may be easier to arrange and suit the purchase better. Unsecured loans are more useful for costs that leave nothing to pledge.
Do I have to give a personal guarantee?

Many lenders ask for one, particularly for smaller companies and larger amounts. It makes a director personally responsible if the company defaults. Some lenders will lend without one, often for smaller sums or stronger accounts. Ask your broker what each lender expects.
What documents will I need?

Usually recent bank statements, the latest filed accounts and sometimes management accounts or forecasts. For larger sums, lenders may ask about your order book or key contracts. Having these ready can make the process smoother. Bank statements show how money moves, which helps a lender judge affordability.
Can I repay the loan early?

Some loans allow early repayment, sometimes with a fee or interest for part of the term, while others do not. Check the early settlement terms before agreeing, particularly if you expect a large customer payment that could clear the debt.
How much could my business borrow?

It depends on revenue, profit, existing debts and trading history rather than a fixed formula. A broker can give a sense of what lenders usually consider for businesses like yours, but no amount is guaranteed until a lender has reviewed your details.

commercial-mortgages|manufacturing.title: Commercial Mortgages for Manufacturers | Loanleaf
commercial-mortgages|manufacturing.desc: How commercial mortgages work for UK manufacturers buying a factory or unit, or releasing cash from premises they own. One short form matches you with a broker.
commercial-mortgages|manufacturing.lead: Buy the unit or factory you operate from, or borrow against premises you own, with repayments spread over many years.
intro: Paying rent on a unit you have outgrown, or one built around your machinery, can feel like paying for someone else’s asset. A commercial mortgage lets a manufacturer buy the premises it occupies, or borrow against a site it already owns, with repayments spread over a long term, commonly 15 to 25 years. Because industrial units vary so much, lenders judge each one individually, and the valuation can differ from the price you have agreed with the seller.

Industrial property brings its own questions. Lenders look at the building’s condition, floor loading, power supply, access and whether it could be let or sold to another occupier if the business failed. For example, a metal fabricator buying a £900,000 unit may need a deposit of a quarter or more. A broker who understands industrial property can explain how lenders are likely to view your site. The broker can explain how the lenders they work with handle energy ratings, planning use and specialist fit-outs.
uses: Buying the unit you rent
Move from paying rent to owning the property, so the monthly cost builds equity instead of ending with the lease.
Moving to a bigger site
Buy larger premises with better loading, higher bays or more power when the current factory limits output.
Releasing cash from owned premises
Borrow against a factory that has risen in value or is mortgage-free, and use the money for equipment or working capital.
Sale and leaseback
Sell the building to an investor or lender and lease it back, freeing the capital while you carry on trading from the same site.
fit: Owner-occupied and specialist premises

Lenders generally treat a unit used by its owner differently from an investment property, and often value it more cautiously if it was built for one process. A general-purpose unit that another business could use is typically easier to finance.
Deposit, term and valuation

Many lenders ask for a deposit or equity of 20 to 40 percent, depending on the property and the business. A formal valuation sets the amount, so the price you agree and the figure a lender values the building at can differ.
What the lender checks about the business

They will look at filed accounts, profit and how comfortably earnings cover the repayments, along with the age of the business. Many ask for a charge over the property and sometimes a personal guarantee from directors.
considerations: Energy efficiency and condition

Commercial premises can face minimum energy performance rules, and an older factory with a poor rating may need upgrades. Lenders may ask about condition and compliance, and you should factor the cost into the purchase.
Tying up capital in a building

A deposit, legal fees and stamp duty land tax come out of cash you could invest in machinery or stock. Think about whether owning the building earns more for the business than that cash would elsewhere.
Long commitment
A mortgage runs for many years, and early repayment may carry charges. If your business may need to move or change shape within a few years, a lease or a shorter-term loan could be more flexible.
faqs: Can I get a commercial mortgage for a unit I already rent?

Yes, buying a unit you currently lease is common. The lender will value the property and look at the business’s accounts. If your landlord is willing to sell, it can simplify matters, although the price and valuation need to line up.
How much deposit will I need?

It varies by lender, property type and your business’s strength. Many ask for somewhere around 20 to 40 percent of the value, and specialist premises may need more. Existing equity in another property can sometimes reduce the cash you need to find.
Can I include machinery in the purchase?

Some lenders will consider fixed plant that is part of the building, but most machinery is financed separately through asset finance. Combining the two can complicate valuation, so a broker may suggest splitting the borrowing. Splitting the borrowing can make each valuation simpler.
What is sale and leaseback?

You sell the building to an investor or lender and lease it back for a set period, releasing the capital tied up in the property. You pay rent, and may not own the building at the end. It suits some businesses but not all.
Do commercial mortgages need a personal guarantee?

Lenders sometimes ask directors to guarantee, particularly for smaller companies or higher loan-to-value borrowing. Larger deposits and stronger accounts can reduce the need. Ask your broker what each lender requires before you apply. A stronger deposit can sometimes reduce what lenders ask for.

asset-finance|transport-and-logistics.h1: Asset finance for hauliers and fleets
asset-finance|transport-and-logistics.title: Asset Finance for Hauliers and Fleets | Loanleaf
asset-finance|transport-and-logistics.desc: How hire purchase and leasing work for UK hauliers, couriers and logistics firms buying HGVs, vans and trailers. One short form matches you with a broker.
asset-finance|transport-and-logistics.lead: Add or replace lorries, vans and trailers and spread the cost over the working life of each vehicle.
intro: A new tractor unit can cost well over £100,000, and a trailer adds tens of thousands more. For a fleet, asset finance lets you pay for each vehicle in instalments while it earns, with the vehicle itself acting as security. The two main routes are hire purchase, where you own the vehicle at the end, and leasing or contract hire, where the lender keeps ownership. Lenders also look at your operator licence and your accounts, so having these in order helps the conversation get started.

How a lender prices the deal depends heavily on what the vehicle will be worth later, which turns on its age, mileage and emissions standard. For example, a courier firm adding five vans for a new parcel contract may prefer contract hire with a fixed monthly cost, while a haulier running trailers for fifteen years may prefer to own them. A broker who works with fleets can compare structures. It also helps to know your replacement cycle so each agreement lines up with how long you will actually keep the vehicle.
uses: Adding vehicles for a contract
Take on extra HGVs, vans or trailers when a customer commits to volumes your current fleet cannot carry.
Meeting emissions and clean air rules
Replace older vehicles that face charges or restrictions in clean air zones, instead of paying the full price at once.
Refreshing the fleet on a cycle
Plan replacements so every vehicle is financed against a known residual value, keeping maintenance and breakdown costs predictable.
Trailers, tail-lifts and specialist bodies
Finance trailers, refrigeration units or tail-lifts, which may be funded alongside the vehicle or on their own.
fit: Residual values and mileage

Lenders consider how much a vehicle will fetch at the end. High-mileage tractor units lose value faster than trailers, so terms are often shorter for lorries and longer for trailers. Agreeing a mileage limit can affect how a lease is priced.
New versus used vehicles

Many lenders will finance used HGVs and vans, usually with a cap on age at the end of the term. Older vehicles may need larger deposits or shorter terms. A broker can say which lenders are comfortable with your usual vehicles.
Balloon payments and structures

Some agreements include a final larger payment, which keeps monthly costs lower but leaves a sum to settle or refinance. Check that the balloon is realistic compared with the likely resale value of the vehicle.
considerations: Operator licence and compliance
Lenders financing HGVs may ask about your operator licence and how many vehicles it covers. Make sure the licence allows for the vehicles you plan to add before you commit to a deal.
Contract hire limits

Leasing and contract hire can come with mileage allowances, condition standards and charges at the end. Heavy use or damage can mean extra costs, so check the terms against how you actually run the fleet.
A vehicle off the road still has to be paid for
Payments continue if a lorry breaks down or sits idle between contracts. Think about whether income from a single contract would cover the repayments if the work ended.
faqs: Can I finance a used HGV?

Yes, many lenders finance used lorries and trailers, though they often set limits on age and mileage and may ask for a larger deposit. The vehicle’s condition and service history also matter. Specialist lenders may be more flexible than high street ones.
Is hire purchase or contract hire better for a haulier?

It depends on how you use the vehicle. Hire purchase suits operators that keep vehicles for years and want to own them. Contract hire can suit fleets that replace often and want predictable costs. Accounting treatment differs, so check with your accountant.
Can I finance trailers separately from the tractor unit?

Yes. Trailers last longer and keep their value better, so they are often financed on longer terms than tractor units. You can arrange them under separate agreements or one package, whichever suits your fleet’s replacement cycle. Ask the broker which structure suits your replacement plans.
Do I need a deposit?

Not always, but many deals involve one, and it is more common for used or specialist vehicles. A larger deposit lowers repayments and can improve the terms offered. The amount depends on the lender, the vehicle and your accounts. Ask your broker how the deposit affects the overall cost.
What if I want to sell a financed vehicle early?

You would usually need to settle the outstanding balance with the lender first, and there may be early settlement charges. With leasing, ending early can be more costly. Check the early exit terms before signing, especially if your contracts might change.

invoice-finance|transport-and-logistics.h1: Invoice finance for haulage and logistics
invoice-finance|transport-and-logistics.title: Invoice Finance for Haulage and Logistics | Loanleaf
invoice-finance|transport-and-logistics.desc: How invoice finance helps UK hauliers and logistics firms pay fuel, drivers and subcontractors while waiting on customers. Matched with a specialist broker.
invoice-finance|transport-and-logistics.lead: Turn delivered loads into cash so fuel, drivers and subcontractors are paid while customers work through 30 to 60 day terms.
intro: Fuel is paid weekly, drivers are paid monthly and subcontractor hauliers often want payment within days. Meanwhile, the customer you delivered for pays 30 to 60 days after invoice. Invoice finance releases most of an invoice’s value once the load is delivered and billed, and pays the balance, less charges, when the customer settles. Some lenders offer it in a way that your customers never see, while others collect directly, and the difference affects both cost and how customers react.

It works well where invoices are regular and customers are established, such as retailers, manufacturers and freight forwarders. For example, a pallet network member invoicing £120,000 a month could draw against those invoices instead of paying for fuel and wages from its own cash. Proof of delivery matters, because lenders want evidence that the work was completed before they will advance against it. Fees vary, so ask for the total cost across a typical month.
uses: Weekly fuel and driver costs
Keep fuel cards, tolls and wages paid on time even when large customers settle late.
Paying subcontractors quickly
Pay owner-drivers or partner hauliers within days, which helps you keep reliable capacity.
Growing without waiting for the first invoice
Take on a new customer or route and fund the extra running costs from existing invoices.
Smoothing a seasonal peak
Cover the extra drivers, hired vehicles and agency staff in busy months before the money comes in.
fit: Proof of delivery and invoicing discipline

Lenders usually want signed proofs of delivery and clear invoices before they advance cash. Firms that already chase PODs promptly and invoice the same week tend to find the process easier. Delays in paperwork mean delays in funds.
Who your customers are

The facility depends mainly on the credit quality of the customers you bill. Established, financially sound customers support higher advances. Lenders may exclude invoices to customers that pay badly, are in dispute, or are connected to your own company.
Selective or whole turnover

Some facilities cover every invoice, others only the invoices you choose to submit. Selective suits firms with a few big customers and uneven needs. Whole turnover can bring a lower cost per invoice but less flexibility.
considerations: Disputes and deductions

Customers may deduct for damage, late delivery or missing paperwork. Lenders may remove disputed invoices from the facility, so the cash can be pulled back. Good records and a quick dispute process reduce the risk.
Fuel is not part of the invoice

The cost of fuel, tolls and wages remains yours to pay in advance. Invoice finance releases cash after the work is billed, so you may still need a short-term buffer for the days between a load and its invoice.
Customer concentration
If one customer makes up most of your invoices, lenders may cap what they advance against that customer. Taking on a second or third customer of similar size can widen what is available.
faqs: Can I finance invoices to freight forwarders?

Often yes. Lenders will look at the forwarder’s credit standing and payment history. Larger, established forwarders are generally easier to finance against than small or new ones. A broker can tell you which lenders are comfortable with the customers you bill.
Do I need proof of delivery for every invoice?

Most lenders ask for it, either with each invoice or on request. The signed POD is evidence that the customer received the goods and the invoice is valid. Electronic PODs are usually accepted, so check how your driver app’s records can be shared.
Can I use invoice finance with a fleet of vehicles on HP?

Yes, in most cases. The vehicles are secured by the asset finance, and invoice finance is secured against the invoices, so the two do not overlap. A lender may ask to see existing agreements to confirm which assets are already pledged.
Will my customers be told?

It depends on the type of facility. With a disclosed arrangement, customers pay the lender directly. With confidential invoice discounting, you keep collecting and customers see no change. Confidential options may need a stronger trading record and different charges. Ask the broker which type is being offered.
How much of the invoice value is advanced?

Lenders usually advance a large share up front, often around 80 to 90 percent, and pay the remainder when the customer pays, less fees. The exact figure depends on the lender, your customers and your trading history, and is never fixed in advance.

unsecured-business-loans|transport-and-l.title: Unsecured Business Loans for Hauliers | Loanleaf
unsecured-business-loans|transport-and-l.desc: How unsecured business loans suit UK hauliers and logistics firms for non-vehicle costs: repairs, driver training, depots and tracking. Matched with a broker.
unsecured-business-loans|transport-and-l.lead: Pay for repairs, driver recruitment, depot upgrades and new contracts without pledging vehicles or property as security.
intro: Many transport costs sit outside the vehicle itself. A gearbox rebuild, a batch of tyres, the cost of training drivers for CPC and HGV licences, a yard resurfacing or a telematics system do not come with something a lender can easily repossess. An unsecured business loan is a fixed sum repaid in instalments with no charge over your fleet or premises. Lenders will also look at the vehicle finance you already carry, since those payments come first.

The lender relies on your accounts, trading record and how comfortably profits cover the payments, and directors are often asked for a personal guarantee. For example, a regional haulier spending £45,000 on driver recruitment and a depot upgrade to mobilise a new contract might use this route to keep its vehicles free for future asset finance. Buying the vehicles themselves usually works better through asset finance. Lenders will also want to see that your income can carry the repayments if one contract ends.
uses: Mobilising a new contract
Pay for extra drivers, uniforms, tracking and a few weeks of running costs before the first invoice is paid.
Driver recruitment and training
Cover agency fees, Driver CPC, HGV licence training and onboarding, which are lost if the driver leaves.
Major repairs and refurbishment
Fund an engine, gearbox or refrigeration unit repair when the cost is too large to absorb from this month’s cash.
Depot, yard and technology
Pay for resurfacing, security, fuel storage, workshop kit or a telematics and routing system.
fit: Amounts and terms in this sector

Unsecured loans for smaller operators often run from about £10,000 to a few hundred thousand pounds, repaid over one to five years. Larger amounts are possible for businesses with strong accounts, but lenders judge each on its own facts.
What lenders look at

Expect questions on filed accounts, recent bank statements and existing vehicle finance, because that borrowing counts against what you can afford. Lenders also look at how steady your contracts are and how much of your income relies on one customer.
Keeping vehicles free for asset finance

Because the loan is not secured, your trucks and trailers remain available for hire purchase or lease deals. Lenders may still count existing commitments, but borrowing without security keeps your options open.
considerations: Personal guarantees
Directors are commonly asked to guarantee unsecured loans, which can put personal assets at risk if the company cannot repay. Read what you are signing and consider taking independent advice.
Cost when vehicles could be the security
Lenders usually price unsecured lending higher than lending against a vehicle. If the need is a lorry, van or trailer, asset finance is likely to be a better match.
Repayments continue in quiet spells
Monthly instalments are fixed even if a contract ends or volumes fall. If your income is uneven, consider whether a revolving facility, repaid as cash arrives, would be easier to manage.
faqs: Can I use an unsecured loan to buy a van?

You can, but asset finance is often more suitable because the vehicle itself can be the security. That may help with approval, term and repayments. An unsecured loan is better kept for costs that leave nothing for a lender to take.
Will existing vehicle finance affect my application?

Yes, lenders count current commitments when they assess affordability. A fleet on hire purchase means regular outgoings that must be covered alongside a new loan. Having your finance agreements and recent management accounts to hand can help. The broker can help you gather those agreements before you apply.
Can I borrow for a new contract before I have been paid?

Many operators do. Lenders may ask for a copy of the contract or customer details to see that income is likely to follow. Lenders will want to understand the contract, but it does not guarantee a decision. It is still the lender’s decision, so ask the broker which documents would help.
Do hauliers need a personal guarantee?

Many lenders ask for one, particularly for smaller companies and larger amounts. Some will lend without, often for smaller sums or stronger accounts. Ask your broker what different lenders expect so you know before applying. Ask your broker whether the lender they suggest asks for a guarantee.
How long does an unsecured loan take to arrange?

Timing varies by lender and how quickly you provide documents, so Loanleaf cannot promise any timescale. Having bank statements and filed accounts ready usually helps the process move along. The broker will explain what each lender needs. Each lender has its own process, so ask the broker what to expect.

revolving-credit-facility|transport-and-.title: Revolving Credit Facilities for Transport Firms | Loanleaf
revolving-credit-facility|transport-and-.desc: How a revolving credit facility helps UK hauliers and logistics firms with fuel price swings, seasonal peaks and uneven payment. Matched with a broker.
revolving-credit-facility|transport-and-.lead: A flexible limit for fuel, tolls and wages that you draw on when costs peak and repay as customers pay.
intro: Transport costs arrive fast and in unpredictable amounts. Diesel prices move week to week, a busy Q4 brings extra agency drivers and hired vehicles, and a customer that pays late can leave a gap of weeks. A revolving credit facility gives you an agreed limit that you can draw on and repay repeatedly, paying charges on the amount used. You decide when to draw, and the charges follow what you use rather than the whole limit, which keeps the cost down in quiet months.

It suits businesses with recurring swings rather than a single big purchase. For example, a courier firm might use a £100,000 facility to cover fuel and temporary drivers from October to December, repaying in January as retailers settle. Unlike a term loan, the available credit returns as you repay. It sits differently from invoice finance, which advances against specific invoices. It is a way to manage timing, not to replace profit, so lenders look at how steadily the business earns.
uses: Fuel price spikes
Cover a sudden rise in diesel costs while contracted rates, or fuel surcharge clauses, catch up.
Peak season labour and hire
Pay for agency drivers, hired vans and extra shifts in the busy months, then repay as the peak earnings arrive.
Bridging late payers
Keep the payroll and supplier payments on schedule when a major customer pays outside agreed terms.
Unplanned costs
Handle short-notice costs such as a tyre bill, an MOT failure or a replacement vehicle hire without raiding the payroll account.
fit: Sizing the limit to the cycle

A sensible limit reflects your peak weekly outgoings and the length of your customers’ payment terms. Lenders also set the figure from turnover, profits and trading history, so the amount offered may differ from the amount you ask for.
Secured and unsecured facilities

Smaller facilities can be unsecured, often with director guarantees. Larger ones may be secured against debtors, vehicles you own outright or other assets, which can raise the limit. The structure affects how the lender monitors the account.
Alongside vehicle finance

Existing hire purchase and lease payments reduce the cash a lender thinks you have free. Share these commitments openly, because a lender who sees the full picture is more likely to set a limit you can use.
considerations: It is not a permanent loan

If you stay close to the limit all year, the facility is covering a structural gap rather than a seasonal one. In that case a broker may suggest a term loan or invoice finance for the underlying need.
Limits can be reviewed
Lenders review facilities, usually annually, and may reduce the limit if trading weakens. Do not build a business plan on credit that could be changed.
Fees beyond interest
Expect an arrangement fee and perhaps a fee on unused credit. Compare the whole cost with an overdraft or invoice finance before choosing.
faqs: Is a revolving facility the same as an overdraft?

Not quite. An overdraft is attached to your current account and is often repayable on demand. A revolving credit facility is normally a separate agreement with set terms and a review date. Features and charges vary, so ask the broker to explain each one.
Can I use it to pay for a new vehicle?

Technically yes, but it uses up credit you need for running costs. A vehicle usually works better under asset finance, where it is the security and the payments run over its working life. Keep the revolving facility for the swings in daily costs.
How quickly can I draw on it?

Once the facility is in place, many lenders let you draw through an online portal or by request. Timing differs by lender, and some require notice. Check how drawdowns work, because the speed you can access cash matters for fuel and wage days.
What happens if I use all the limit?

You cannot draw more until you repay some of it. If you regularly hit the limit, tell your lender or broker early, because it may point to needing a larger facility or a different type of finance for part of the need.
Will I need to give a personal guarantee?

Often, yes, particularly for smaller or unsecured facilities. Larger facilities backed by assets may not need one. It varies by lender, so ask before you apply. The broker can explain the options and what they may ask of directors. The broker can explain which is likely for your size of facility.

vat-and-tax-loans|transport-and-logistic.h1: VAT and tax loans for hauliers
vat-and-tax-loans|transport-and-logistic.title: VAT and Tax Loans for Hauliers and Logistics | Loanleaf
vat-and-tax-loans|transport-and-logistic.desc: How VAT and tax loans help UK hauliers and logistics firms spread quarterly VAT, PAYE and corporation tax bills. One short form matches you with a broker.
vat-and-tax-loans|transport-and-logistic.lead: Spread a large VAT, PAYE or corporation tax bill into manageable payments instead of draining the cash you need for fuel and wages.
intro: A haulier’s quarterly VAT bill can land at the same time as a big fuel invoice and a payroll run. VAT on vehicles, fuel and maintenance can be recovered, but only as part of the return, so timing can leave you paying out before it comes back. A VAT and tax loan pays HMRC on time and lets the business repay the lender in instalments. Interest and late-payment penalties from HMRC can add up quickly, so having a way to pay on time has real value.

This can help when your cash is tied up in unpaid customer invoices or a recent vehicle purchase. For example, a logistics firm facing a £70,000 VAT bill in a month when two major customers have not yet paid could borrow to settle HMRC on time and repay over several months. Some international haulage is zero-rated, which changes when VAT is paid or reclaimed, so your accountant should confirm your own position.
uses: A quarterly VAT payment
Pay the return on time when customer payments arrive after the due date.
PAYE and National Insurance
Cover a payroll tax bill in a month where wages and fuel have taken the available cash.
Corporation tax
Spread the annual corporation tax bill after a strong year when cash has gone into vehicles or a depot.
Clearing a bill you have fallen behind on
Settle an overdue tax debt to avoid further penalties and interest, where a lender is willing to consider it.
fit: How the loan is structured

Lenders typically advance an amount close to the tax due, repaid over a few months up to a year or two. Some are structured as a short-term loan, while others allow a larger spread. The best option depends on how soon the cash will recover.
Why timing matters in transport

Haulage cash flow is uneven, with fuel and wages paid ahead of customer receipts. If you expect payments soon, a short facility may be enough. If margins are thin all year, a longer repayment period or a different fix may be better.
What lenders look at

Lenders will want recent bank statements, your accounts and details of the tax bill, and they will ask about existing HMRC arrangements. They tend to prefer a bill that is due rather than long overdue, and a business with steady trading.
considerations: Borrowing to pay tax adds cost
You repay the tax and the lender’s charges, so the total paid is higher. Compare this with HMRC’s own Time to Pay arrangements, which may be available and are worth asking about before borrowing.
It does not fix a structural gap
If tax bills keep outrunning cash, a loan may postpone the problem. Look at pricing, payment terms and the cost of running each vehicle to see where the shortfall comes from.
Check the figure with your accountant
VAT schemes, reverse charge rules and zero-rated work affect what you owe. Make sure the amount borrowed matches the actual liability, and that you plan for the next bill as well as this one.
faqs: Can I borrow to pay an HMRC bill that is already overdue?

Some lenders will consider it, though options narrow the longer a bill has been outstanding, and terms may differ. Contact HMRC as well, since they may agree a payment plan. A broker can explain which lenders are open to overdue tax.
Is a VAT loan cheaper than a Time to Pay arrangement?

It depends. HMRC charges interest on late payments and may add penalties, while a loan carries the lender’s charges. Time to Pay arrangements are agreed case by case and are not guaranteed. Compare the full cost of each option before deciding.
Can I use it for fuel duty or vehicle excise?

Fuel duty is built into the pump price, so it is not a separate bill you pay. Vehicle excise duty is a small, regular cost. The loans described here are aimed at larger bills such as VAT, PAYE and corporation tax.
Will the loan be secured?

It may be unsecured, often with a director’s personal guarantee, or secured against assets such as unencumbered vehicles or property. Secured options can allow larger amounts or lower costs. The broker can explain what each lender asks for. Security can widen the options.
How do I know how much to borrow?

Work from your actual liability, using your VAT return or tax calculation, and check it with your accountant. Borrowing only what you need keeps repayments lower. The lender will want to see the bill, so have the figures to hand. Lenders may also ask for your accountant’s figures.

secured-business-loans|transport-and-log.title: Secured Business Loans for Hauliers | Loanleaf
secured-business-loans|transport-and-log.desc: How secured business loans work for UK hauliers and logistics firms, using a depot, yard or owned vehicles as security for larger sums. Matched with a broker.
secured-business-loans|transport-and-log.lead: Borrow a larger sum over a longer term by offering your depot, yard or vehicles you own outright as security.
intro: Some transport projects are bigger than a single vehicle or a short-term cash need: buying a depot, acquiring a smaller haulier’s contracts and fleet, refreshing twenty vehicles at once or building a workshop and fuel storage. A secured business loan gives the lender a legal charge over an asset, which can mean larger sums and longer terms than borrowing without security. Lenders will want a valuation first and will check for existing charges, so it helps to know what you already owe against each asset.

Hauliers often have security to offer. A depot or yard owned outright is the strongest, followed by trailers and vehicles that are fully paid for, or a director’s property. For example, a haulier that owns its yard might borrow £500,000 against it to buy a competitor’s book of work. Because the asset is at risk if repayments fall behind, the loan needs to fit comfortably within what the business reliably earns.
uses: Buying a depot or yard
Fund the purchase of a site with better access, more parking and room for a workshop, using the site and other assets as security.
Acquiring another haulier
Pay for a competitor’s fleet, drivers and contracts where the price is more than the business can fund from cash.
Refreshing a large part of the fleet
Replace many vehicles at once, using a charge over property to access a larger sum than vehicle-by-vehicle finance would give.
Raising cash against owned assets
Borrow against a yard or trailers that are fully paid for and use the money for working capital or growth.
fit: What counts as security

Property is the most widely accepted. Vehicles and trailers you own outright can also be used, but they lose value with mileage and age, so lenders tend to value them cautiously. A mixture of property and vehicles can support a larger loan.
Loan to value and existing charges

Lenders lend a share of an asset’s value, not all of it, and look at any charges already on it. If your yard has a mortgage, a second charge may be possible depending on the equity and the first lender’s consent.
Terms and structure

Property-backed loans can run for ten years or more, while loans against vehicles are usually shorter. A longer term lowers monthly payments but costs more in total. A broker can compare structures and explain what the lender would require.
considerations: The asset is at risk
If repayments are missed, the lender can take action against the property or vehicles. Think carefully about a loss of a major contract before pledging the depot your whole operation depends on.
Vehicle security loses value
A lorry bought five years ago is worth less now than when it was bought. Lenders account for this in what they lend and may ask for extra security as vehicles age.
Costs and time
Valuations, legal work and arrangement fees add cost and take time. Having title documents, vehicle registrations and recent accounts ready can help.
faqs: Can I use my vehicles as security for a loan?

Yes, if you own them outright. Lenders will value them independently and tend to be cautious as vehicles age and mileage builds up. Vehicles already under hire purchase are not available because the lender behind them holds the claim. The vehicle’s age and condition affect the amount.
Will a lender take my depot as security?

Many do, especially for industrial or storage property that other occupiers could use. The lender will value it and check ownership, planning use and any existing charges. Specialist or very remote sites may be valued more cautiously. Yards with good access and no planning limits tend to be easier.
How is a secured loan different from asset finance?

Asset finance funds a particular vehicle with that vehicle as security. A secured loan raises a general sum against property or other assets, and can be used more flexibly, for example to buy a depot or another business. Each fits different needs, and a broker can compare them for you.
Do I need a personal guarantee as well?

Sometimes. Lenders may ask for a director’s guarantee or a charge over a personal property, even with business security. It depends on the loan size and the strength of the business. Ask your broker what each lender requires. Guarantees can sometimes be limited in amount, so ask.
Can I borrow against a depot I rent?

Not against the land, since you do not own it. A lender may look at other assets or consider a different type of finance. If you are thinking of buying the site, a commercial mortgage may be a better route.
